en: O Dharmadhātu, homage to you, the Dharmadhātu, who abide within all sentient beings;
it is through lack of full knowledge of you that they wander in the abode of the three realms of existence.
That very same element which is being purified within saṃsāra is indeed that very same thing when pure;
for it is that very same thing which is the dharmakāya in nirvāṇa.
(2) Just as the cream of clarified butter mixed with milk is not seen, so too the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) mixed with afflictions is not seen.
(3) Just as milk, when thoroughly purified, becomes the substance of ghee that is perfectly stainless,
so too the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), when purified of afflictions, is perfectly stainless.
(4) Just as a lamp situated inside a jar does not illuminate anything at all,
so too the dharmadhātu, when situated within the jar of the afflictions, does not shine forth.
(5) For from whichever side that jar has a hole,
from that very side its rays have emerged.
(6) When that jar is shattered by the vajra of meditative concentration,
it shines forth everywhere, extending to the limits of space.
(7) The realm of phenomena is neither arisen nor ceased at any time;
it is forever undefiled, pure in its beginning, middle, and end.
(8) Just as a lapis lazuli gem, though radiant at all times,
does not have its luster shine when it is concealed within a covering of stone.
(9) For in this way, the utterly stainless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), when shrouded by afflictions, does not shine in saṃsāra; yet in nirvāṇa, it is luminous.
(10) When the lineage exists, there is exertion, as illustrated by the example of gold;
when the lineage does not exist, exertion is held to be nothing but mere fatigue.
(11) Just as grain covered by husks is not considered to be the actual fruit,
so too one who is shrouded by afflictions is not conceived of as a Buddha.
(12) Just as that fruit appears when it is freed from its husk,
so indeed does the Dharma-body shine forth when it is freed from afflictions.
(13) An analogy is made in the world by means of the plantain tree, which has no core;
yet its fruits are substantial and are eaten as if they were like nectar.
(14) For thus, when this essence-less saṃsāra has been stilled within the ocean of afflictions,
even his fruit is Buddhahood— the nectar for all embodied beings.
(15) For in this way, from all seeds, a fruit arises that is similar [to them].
Without seeds there is no fruit; what wise person would accept [otherwise]?
(16) This element, being the seed of all phenomena, is considered their basis;
when purified in this gradual manner, it brings about the state of Buddhahood.
(17) Indeed, the stainless moon and sun are obscured by five kinds of impurities:
by clouds, mist, smoke, the mouth of Rāhu, dust, and so forth.
(18) Thus the luminous mind is obscured by five impurities: sensual desire, ill will, torpor, restlessness, and doubt.
(19) (4) Just as a garment soiled with various impurities becomes pure through fire— when it is cast into the midst of the fire, the impurity is burned away, yet the nature of the cloth remains.
(20) Thus the mind, though luminous, is defiled by stains born of passion;
when the stain is burned by the fire of gnosis, that luminosity itself is not burned.
(21) Whatever sūtras teaching emptiness have been spoken by the Victors,
by all of them there is the turning away of the afflictions, and never the destruction of the element.
Just as water hidden within the earth remains pure,
so too does knowledge, though obscured by afflictions, shine forth perfectly stainless.
(23) Since the *dharmadhātu* is neither self, nor female, nor male, nor neuter,
and is entirely free from all grasping, how can it be conceptualized as a "self"?
(24) For all phenomena are indeed unattached; for femininity and masculinity do not exist. Femininity and masculinity are displayed only for the sake of training those blinded by passion.
(25) There are three mental contemplations: that [all things] are impermanent, suffering, and empty.
The supreme mental contemplation is the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena.
(26) Just as an embryo exists within a pregnant woman yet is not seen,
so too the reality of phenomena, shrouded by afflictions, is not seen.

(27) For the arising of the four kinds of conceptualization occurs from the primary elements and their derivatives; indeed, the conceptualization of "I" and "mine" is born from names, notions, and signs.
(28) For the vow of the Buddhas is without appearance and without characteristics; because it is to be personally realized by yogins, it is the eternal nature of the Buddhas.
(29) Just as a hare's horn, when conceptualized, does not exist,
so too among all phenomena, that which is conceptually constructed does not exist at all.
(30) There is the atom-dust, yet the cow's horn does not exist;
as it was before, so it is after—what can be conceived of that by the wise?
(31) It arises precisely by depending [on conditions] and ceases by depending [on conditions].
There is no coming-into-being of a single [independent entity]; how is it conceptualized by the foolish?
(32) (7) Having seen that both the hare's horn and the cow's horn are characterized by conceptual construction,
one should proceed according to the Middle Way, which is the true nature of the Sugata’s Dharma.
(33) Just as the reflection of the moon, the sun, and the stars is seen in a clear vessel of water, so indeed is the perfected nature.
(34) It is good in the beginning, middle, and end, non-deceptive, and eternal;
for one whose self is of such a nature, how can it be conceptualized as a "self"?
(35) Just as water is called "hot" during the summer season,
yet that very same water is called "cold" during the winter seasons.
(36) When the mind is enveloped by the net of afflictions, it is called "citta";
that very same [mind], through the departure of afflictions, is called "Buddha."
(37) Depending upon the eye and forms, and through utterly pure illuminations, those [illuminations] are unarisen and unceasing; understand them as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
(38) Depending upon the ear and sound, the mind and the three types of representation arise;
by means of one's own conceptual construction, the signless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is heard.
(39) The nose is dependent on odors; the olfactory faculty is formless and invisible.
The suchness of olfactory consciousness is conceptualized as the dharma-realm.
(40) For the tongue is empty of intrinsic nature, and the element of taste is solitude;
(9) non-abiding consciousness is the very nature of the dharma-realm.
(41) Having the nature of the pure body, characterized by the condition of contact, yet liberated from conditions— I call that the *dharmadhātu*.
(42) When the mind is free from the imagined and the imagining regarding the primary phenomena,
the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena is realized as the dharmadhātu.
The yogi sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, and discerns phenomena; such is the characteristic of the perfected state.
The eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and likewise the mind—
this pure sixfold sense-base is the characteristic of reality.
(45) (10) Mind alone is seen to be twofold: that which is mundane and that which is supramundane.
Through the grasping at a self comes saṃsāra; yet, when realized within oneself, it is indeed suchness.
(46) For nirvāṇa is the destruction of attachment, as well as the destruction of hatred and delusion;
for the sake of awakening to that, Buddhahood is the refuge of all embodied beings.
Within this body, all that is both knowledge and ignorance;
one is bound by one's own conceptual construction and liberated by thorough self-cognition.
(48) Awakening is neither distant nor near; it has neither gone nor come.
It is not seen, and yet it is indeed seen right here within this very cage of afflictions.
And it is said in the collections of sūtras: "The one who contemplates the self dwells by means of the dwelling of the lamp of wisdom, having attained supreme peace."
(50) One should not have the perception that awakening is distant, nor should one perceive it as near;
for by thoroughly understanding, as they truly are, the appearances of the objects of the six [senses], [one realizes awakening].
Just as when milk is mixed with water in a single vessel,
the swans drink the milk while leaving the water as it remains.
(52) For in this way, yogins drink from a single vessel the knowledge mixed with afflictions; they manifest both knowledge and ignorance.
(53) As long as the external world is conceptualized through the grasping of "I" or "mine," so long does the seed of existence persist;
but when the selflessness of objects is perceived,
that seed of existence is extinguished.
For the Buddha indeed enters parinirvāṇa, being pure and the eternal abode of auspiciousness;
the foolish conceptualize duality, whereas non-duality is the state of the yogins.
(55) Through various difficult practices, through gifts, through ethical discipline, through gathering beings for their welfare,
and through patience that assists sentient beings— this nourishment of the element is threefold.
(56) Diligence in all dharmas, the mind directed toward meditative concentration,
and being constantly immovable in wisdom— this, moreover, is the nourishment of awakening.
Wisdom conjoined with skillful means and purified by aspirational prayers;
knowledge well-established in the powers; and the fourfold nourishment of the elements.
(58) "Do not pay homage to the Bodhisattvas"—this was an exceedingly ill-spoken word.
[He] spoke thus regarding the Bodhisattva Ajīva... (59) ... [omission] ... (60)
Having placed [the materials] here, one should reflect:
"The production of jaggery, sugar, and candied sugar occurs there."
(61) For when the bodhicitta is protected, one should reflect upon this with focused attention:
the arising of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas occurs therein.
(62) Just as farmers provide protection for rice sprouts and the like, so do the Leaders provide protection for those who are devoted to the [Buddha] body.

(63) Just as the form of the moon is seen on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, so too is the form of the Buddha seen by those who have faith in the supreme vehicle. (64) Just as the growth of the young moon is observed moment by moment, [so too is the growth of the bodhisattva].
Likewise, for those who have entered the stages, an increase is seen moment by moment.
(65) Just as indeed on the fifteenth day the full moon arises,
so too upon the stage that has reached the culmination, the Dharmakāya arises.
(66) He whose resolve regarding the Buddha and the Dharma is always firm generates that irreversible mind in birth after birth.
(67) When there is the transformation of the basis that was dark and the acquisition of the basis that is white,
(15) then, through the awakening to that, it is designated as "Joy" (muditā).
(68) For it is indeed always defiled by various impurities such as passion and the like;
and that purity which occurs in the absence of impurity is designated as "stainless."
(69) Through the cessation of the web of afflictions, it is stainless and brilliantly radiant;
through the departure of immeasurable darkness, it is indeed the Luminous One.
Pure, eternally luminous, and entirely free from those things born of attachment,
the stage surrounded by the flames of gnosis is considered the Radiant (Arciṣmatī).
(71) There is indeed a manifold variety of all sciences, arts, crafts, and meditations;
yet the victory over the afflictions that are difficult to conquer is exceedingly hard to win.
(72) This stage, Abhimukhī, which is profound in its arising and passing away, encompasses all perfections and all three types of enlightenment.
(73) (16) It sports with a web of rays and circular arrays on all sides;
having crossed the flood of mud from the three worlds, it is known as the "Far-Reaching" (Dūraṅgamā).
(74) Sustained by the Buddhas, he has entered the ocean of gnosis;
having attained mastery over effortlessness, he is unshakable by the servants of Māra.
(75) Having reached the perfection in all the analytical knowledges through the teaching of the Dharma and philosophical discussions, that yogi is said to be on the stage known as Sādhumatī.
(76) The Cloud of Dharma of the Buddhas sustains everywhere the delightful body composed of gnosis, which is as stainless as space. (77) It is the support of all phenomena. (17)
The appropriation of the fruit of practice is called the transformation of the basis, which is the Dharma-body.
(78) That which is free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is inconceivable, while that which possesses the latent impressions of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is conceivable.
You are inconceivable to all; who is capable of knowing you?

(79) You who transcend the domain of all speech, who are beyond the range of all sense faculties, and who are accessible only to mental consciousness— whatever you are, whatever you are, homage be to you!
(80) Gradually brought to full accomplishment, the sons of the Buddha, possessed of great renown,
perceive the emptiness of the true nature of phenomena through the wisdom of the Cloud of Dharma.
(81) When the mind has been cleansed and has crossed over the ocean of existence,
(18) his seat, consisting of a great lotus, becomes firmly established.
(82) It has the luster of many jeweled petals, is radiant with its auspicious marks,
and is surrounded on all sides by many tens of millions of lotuses.
(83) By means of the ten powers, the Child remains like the young moon;
yet, due to the afflictions of beings whose minds are defiled, he does not see the Tathāgata.

(84) Just as when hungry ghosts see the ocean as dry on all sides, so too for those consumed by ignorance, there arises the conceptualization that "the Buddha does not exist. (85) What can the Blessed One do for beings of little merit? [Their] birth... (19)
